title: Enhancing Quality and Security in CI: Gunjan Patel

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk's primary focus is AI agents in CI pipelines that review code, generate unit tests, identify security issues, and propose fixes. The system is a CI-based code review assistant for software engineers, shared as developer tooling templates with bring-your-own-LLM. The system is a side project with several unimplemented features and CI templates not yet uploaded at talk time. The talk assumes knowledge of CI/CD pipelines and LLM prompting but remains accessible to practitioners. Recorded conference presentation at the AI Engineer World's Fair in San Francisco. summary: Gunjan Patel, Director of Engineering at Palo Alto Networks, explores using AI in CI/CD pipelines to automate code improvement — a side project, not a company product. He opens by referencing the concept of "Flow": developers stay productive when challenge matches skill, but mundane tasks like unit tests and documentation drop them into boredom. His thesis is to outsource these boring tasks to CI using what he calls a "ghost pilot" — a deliberate, slow AI code reviewer contrasted with fast, just-in-time co-pilots like GitHub Copilot. He draws on Kahneman's "Thinking Fast and Slow" as an analogy. The ghost pilot architecture has four sequential CI steps. First, it improves variable names and code comments so subsequent AI steps draw on broader LLM knowledge — for example, renaming "rev" to "annual revenue" lets the model pull in finance-domain edge cases. Second, it iteratively adds unit tests: an LLM first infers expected behavior, then adopts an adversarial mindset to list boundary and edge cases, personalizes additions using team priorities stored in context.yaml and historical Jira bugs, and finally generates and loops tests until they pass. Third, it uses environmental context (cloud provider, PII presence, deployment type, security policies, PRD, Slack, Jira) to identify security issues beyond what SAST tools catch, including logical-flow problems. For security analysis, he simulates three AI employees — a red team engineer, a Python developer, and an engineering manager — who take turns debating each security finding's risk, priority, and effort, then self-reflect on conclusions. He references research showing this multi-path simulation approach is more effective than standard LLM use. A Kubernetes bug example demonstrates the system finding a critical logical vulnerability — a misplaced safe statement — that postdated GPT-3.5's training cutoff and would not be caught by SAST tools. Fourth, the system proposes fixes for human review, summarizing the three-persona debate in three bullet points with risk scores, effort scores, code snippets, and security policy citations. Unit tests are re-run before human review to establish a baseline so reviewers don't waste time verifying fixes. He dedicates the talk to his late friend Nikhil and plans to share CI templates (GitLab CI and GitHub Actions) on his GitHub repo.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: "Ghost pilots" are deliberate, slow AI code reviewers in CI, contrasting with fast, just-in-time developer co-pilots like GitHub Copilot.
Improving variable names and code comments early in CI helps subsequent AI steps leverage broader LLM domain knowledge and understand developer intent.
Unit test generation is iterative: infer expected behavior, adopt adversarial mindset for edge cases, personalize from team priorities and historical bugs, then generate and loop until passing.
Context is assembled from both user-provided sources (context.yaml, PRD, Jira, Slack, security policies) and AI-inferred sources (language type, historical bug patterns).

Security analysis simulates three AI personas (red team engineer, Python developer, engineering manager) in a multi-turn debate to prioritize findings, with research showing this is more effective than standard LLM use.
The system proposes fixes for human review with risk scores, effort scores, code snippets, and security policy citations, then re-runs unit tests before review.
AI in CI can find logical-flow vulnerabilities that SAST tools miss, demonstrated with a Kubernetes bug postdating GPT-3.5's training cutoff.
AI in CI can leverage longer processing time since CI jobs aren't constrained by developer impatience for instant responses.
AI tends to always find issues when asked — requiring prioritization logic to distinguish critical from trivial findings.

sections.title: Introduction and Dedication
sections.summary: Gunjan Patel introduces himself as Director of Engineering at Palo Alto Networks, clarifies this is a side project not a company product, and dedicates the talk to his late friend Nikhil who passed away unexpectedly two weeks prior.

sections.title: Developer Flow and Boring Tasks
sections.summary: References the book 'Flow' describing the optimal zone where skill matches challenge. Developers start productive but drop into boredom when writing unit tests and documentation. The thesis is to outsource these boring tasks to CI, giving developers more time to write code.

sections.title: Co-pilot vs Ghost Pilot
sections.summary: Distinguishes co-pilots (fast, just-in-time, developer-facing, measured by response speed) from ghost pilots (slow, deliberate, iterative, context-aware code review). Draws analogy to Kahneman's Thinking Fast and Slow.

sections.title: High-Level CI Architecture
sections.summary: Presents a four-step CI pipeline: (1) improve variable names and code comments, (2) add and run unit tests in a loop, (3) identify security issues from environmental context, (4) propose fixes for human review and re-run tests.

sections.title: Improving Variable Names and Code Comments
sections.summary: Explains why improving variable names helps LLMs leverage broader domain knowledge (e.g., 'rev' to 'annual revenue'), and why updated code comments clarify developer intent, which is important since code may have bugs but intent is clear. Shows example of 'port' improved to 'port number'.

sections.title: Iterative Unit Test Generation
sections.summary: Describes a multi-step iterative unit test process: LLM infers expected behavior as baseline, adopts adversarial mindset to list edge/boundary cases, personalizes tests from team priorities and historical Jira bugs, then generates and loops until tests pass. Emphasizes CI has time for iteration unlike ID-based assistants.

sections.title: Building Context for AI
sections.summary: Details context sources: user-provided (context.yaml with cloud provider, service type, PII presence, frontend/backend, PRD, Jira, Slack, security policies) and AI-inferred (language type, focus areas from historical bugs). Notes a planned but unimplemented follow-up question feature. References opencontext.org as potential integration.

sections.title: Security: Three AI Employees Debate
sections.summary: Simulates three AI personas — red team engineer (security policies, code), Python developer (author identity, PRD), and engineering manager (business context, Slack, Zoom, PRD) — who take turns debating each security finding's risk, priority, and effort, then self-reflect. Goes beyond SAST by finding logical-flow issues and company-policy violations.

sections.title: Security Fix Proposals and Closing
sections.summary: Describes the fix proposal step: outcome-based suggestions with risk scores, effort scores, code snippets, and security policy citations, summarized in three bullet points from the AI personas' debate. Unit tests re-run before human review to establish baseline. Demonstrates with a Kubernetes bug — a critical logical vulnerability (misplaced safe statement) postdating GPT-3.5's training cutoff, not caught by SAST. Shows a hardcoded API key fix example. References research showing multi-path simulation is more effective than standard LLM use. Closes by sharing his GitHub repo where GitLab CI and GitHub Actions templates will be uploaded.
